A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OSDFace, with matching core methods and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 adds a separately numbered supplement, which was included in this assessment.

before.justification: v1 reports original face-restoration results on synthetic and real-world datasets, computational measurements, and component ablations in Tables 1–5.

after.justification: v2 retains original restoration experiments and adds VRE-transfer experiments, parallel-inference measurements, recognition tests under atmospheric turbulence, and cartoon-restoration examples.

M1.justification: The core OSDFace architecture, two-stage training, and losses remain unchanged. Supplementary Sections B–C add an evaluated procedure that executes the prompt embedder and VAE encoder in parallel, and an OSEDiff*+VRE adaptation integrating VRE into another restoration model.

E1.justification: v2 adds zero-shot cartoon restoration using Anime Face Dataset (main Figure 6) and downstream LFW face recognition under previously unseen atmospheric turbulence (Supplementary Section D). These substantially extend the evaluated domain, task requirements, and degradation conditions beyond the retained restoration benchmarks.

E2.justification: The original restoration comparator set is retained. Supplementary Tables 2–3 add OSEDiff*+VRE to comparisons against OSDFace. The new recognition experiment also includes a no-restoration control alongside DAEFR, DiffBIR, and OSEDiff*.

E3.justification: The new recognition protocol evaluates 3,000 positive and 3,000 negative LFW pairs at turbulence propagation lengths of 20,000, 30,000, and 40,000, reporting PR, ROC, F1, and similarity-separation measurements. Supplementary Section B also compares serialized and parallel execution. Existing main-text training and restoration-evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds experiments testing whether VRE improves OSEDiff, recognition robustness across unseen turbulence severities, and the computational benefit of parallel execution. Supplementary Section F adds case analyses involving occlusions, profiles, multiple faces, accessories, and backgrounds. The original prompt and loss ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new recognition curves and mean-distance bars introduce evaluation measurements without adding uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The unstarred OSEDiff scores change throughout main Tables 1–2. For example, CelebA-Test LPIPS changes from 0.4708 to 0.3306, overtaking OSDFace's unchanged 0.3365; the reason for this revision is unspecified. v2 also adds VRE-transfer results, serialized/parallel timings, recognition curves, and qualitative outputs. The original OSDFace benchmark scores and main ablation results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Supplementary Figure 3 newly defines mean sample distance as the difference between average cosine similarities for predicted positive and negative pairs. This is a limited mathematical-definition addition associated with evaluation. The original diffusion and loss equations remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims: one-step face restoration, VRE-based visual conditioning, identity and distribution alignment, and strong quality with efficient inference. Additional experiments support these claims without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: Supplementary Section E adds specific limitations involving color shifts, skin textures and non-facial regions such as fingers, and minimally degraded inputs, including explanations tied to training coverage. Sections C–D also interpret VRE transfer and downstream recognition benefits. v1 lacks this substantive discussion of applicability and failure conditions.

D1.justification: v2 identifies the recognition evaluator as the official ArcFace MS1MV3 R50 model, describes parallel execution, and clarifies that existing OSEDiff* retraining uses OSDFace's dataset and experimental settings. Core training details remain unchanged, and both versions still promise future code and model release.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for Anime Face Dataset, DialogueNeRF, atmospheric-turbulence simulation, and AdaIN. The DFOSD-to-D3SR rename matches the same arXiv:2410.04224 reference. The main related-work discussion and positioning remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 lightly edits main-text wording, updates terminology, adds acknowledgments, and organizes additional material into Supplementary Sections A–F. The original section order, narrative, and method exposition are largely retained; there is no extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds a cartoon-restoration figure, supplementary comparison and timing tables, a multi-panel recognition figure, and extensive synthetic and real-world comparison grids. Main Figure 3 gains explicit component labels, and Table 1 is resized beside the cartoon examples. These substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: The supplement substantially strengthens validation by testing VRE in another model and evaluating downstream identity recognition under unseen degradation. Concrete failure conditions also make the paper's applicability clearer than in v1. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: the OSEDiff score revisions are unexplained, and Section 4.2 retains an LPIPS-superiority statement inconsistent with revised Table 1.
